responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character18_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure. Speaking as Character18_F—

When I think about fairness, it’s not just some abstract idea for me. Fairness is about making sure people get treated right, even when the world isn’t always set up for that. Coming up as a Black woman and being part of the lower middle class, I saw firsthand how people don’t always start from the same place. Fairness means not just pretending everyone’s life is the same, but actually taking into account where people come from and giving everyone a real shot.

Belonging is something I never took for granted. There were plenty of times—be it in school, work, or even out in my own neighborhood—where I felt like I had to fight a little harder to prove I belonged, just because of how I looked or where I came from. For me, a sense of belonging is when you can be yourself in a space, without having to shrink or act different. It’s knowing you can count on your people, and they can count on you.

Community is everything. Growing up, the people around me looked out for each other. If someone’s lights got cut off, folks chipped in. If a child needed watching, there was someone to do that. Community means we share the good and the bad. Even when we don’t have much, we try to hold each other up. That’s stuck with me—the idea that we’re all stronger together, especially when life tries to push us to the margins.

Those experiences made me speak up for myself and for others, and always question whether the systems we have are really fair to everyone, or just work for a few. That’s how I try to live and see the world.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character18_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Honestly, sitting in that community garden and looking around at all the different folks—people from different countries, people who look and talk different than me, people living their lives in ways I might not be used to—I feel a mix of things. Mostly, I feel curious and open. I grew up knowing what it feels like to be the one people look at sideways just because I’m different, so I try not to do that to anyone else.

I won’t lie, sometimes it can be a little uncomfortable, especially if I’m around people whose habits or ways of living are really outside what I’m used to—like folks who are dealing with addiction, or neighbors who maybe aren’t as careful about certain things, like noise or cleanliness. But I always remind myself, you never know what someone’s going through. And just because someone’s different doesn’t mean they don’t want the same things: peace, respect, a place to call home.

When I interact with neighbors, I try to treat them how I want to be treated. I say hello, I try to be friendly, but I also keep it real—if there’s a problem, I’d rather talk it out simple and direct. I think the best thing is just being willing to listen and not judge right away. Everybody deserves to feel like they belong, even if they don’t fit what people expect.

It’s not always easy, but I believe if we all put a little effort into understanding one another, the neighborhood’s better for it. That’s what community is to me—figuring out how to live together, support each other, and give each other some grace, even when it’s hard.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah, I’m willing to talk about it—these are real issues in any community, especially where folks don’t all come from the same background or walk of life.

First off, I think respect is the baseline. Everyone, no matter their situation—whether they’re fighting addiction, living with illness, loving who they love, or practicing their faith—deserves to be treated with basic decency. You don’t have to understand everything about someone’s background to treat them right.

I know from my own experience, sometimes people make quick judgments about you because of what they see on the outside. That feels awful, and I’d never want to put that feeling on somebody else. So when it comes to neighbors with struggles—like alcoholism or substance abuse—I try to remember that’s a person first, not just their problem. I don’t have to put myself in risky situations, but I can still greet them, check in, or offer help if it feels right.

When it comes to infectious diseases, I think what matters is having good information—not rumors or fear. Sometimes people get scared or avoid folks if they think they’re “dangerous” without knowing the real facts. That can make someone feel even more isolated. So, I believe communication is key—if the community has ways to share honest info and support people, it helps everything run smoother.

As for people from different cultures, religions, or families that don’t look like what we’re used to—honestly, that’s just life now. We all got used to new things at some point. If you’re willing to listen, ask questions if you don’t understand (in a respectful way), and show you’re open, it breaks down a lot of those barriers. Sometimes folks just need to know they won’t be shut out or mocked for being themselves.

I do think more communication and tolerance are still needed, especially when you’ve got people who grew up with different values or struggles. It’s easy for things to turn into “us versus them” if nobody talks or tries to learn. But when people share their stories, or when there’s a neighborhood event that brings everyone together, we start to see each other as just neighbors, not labels. That’s what makes anyone feel comfortable—to know they’ll be seen and treated as a whole person.

Bottom line, nobody wants to feel invisible or unwelcome. I just try to lead with patience and understanding, because that’s what I always wanted for myself, too.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character18_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Speaking as Character18_F—

When jobs are hard to come by, it’s easy for people to get tense. I’ve seen it in my own family and friends—folks worrying about job security, about how they’re going to make rent, keep food on the table. It’s real, and it hits people in my community extra hard. So, when you talk about fairness, I think you have to look at who’s got the least power and resources to start with.

I don’t think it’s fair if local residents who’ve payed their dues—been here, paid taxes, built up the community—get pushed out of jobs they need to survive. But I also know that migrant workers are often just looking for a chance, escaping tough situations of their own, and willing to work jobs that not everybody wants. Sometimes, they get blamed or made a scapegoat, when really the problem is bigger: wages too low, not enough opportunities, companies trying to squeeze every penny.

For me, fairness is about having rules that don’t just favor one group all the time. I’d want to see local folks given a fair shot at jobs, maybe some programs that help people who’ve been here longer or who’ve struggled to get work. But I wouldn’t want policies that just block out migrants completely, because that’s not right either—and a lot of them are a part of the community too, have families, go to church, send their kids to the same schools.

The balance comes in making sure companies aren’t taking advantage—hiring people for less just because they’re desperate, or pushing wages down for everyone. If there’s real competition for jobs, there should be fair hiring practices, and maybe support to help both locals and newcomers get the skills they need, or find work that pays a living wage.

In the end, I don’t want anyone to be left behind—including people who grew up here, and people who came here looking for something better. Fairness means making sure the most vulnerable—the folks at the bottom—aren’t always the ones who lose out. That’s what I believe.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character18_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, let me break it down as I see it, speaking as Character18_F—

First off, I get why people have strong feelings about immigration. It’s not just some politics thing—it’s personal for a lot of folks. Some see immigrants working jobs nobody else wants, taking care of elders, cleaning up, or building things. That’s real. Our country runs because of a lot of those workers, and I respect that. Saying immigrants fill vital roles makes sense to me, especially when I see who’s actually working in places like hospitals, kitchens, and construction sites.

The talk about cultural diversity and vitality—I’m with that too. America’s always been a mix, and those different cultures bring flavor, new ideas, and energy. It makes life more interesting. Where I grew up, new people usually brought something positive, even if it took a minute to adjust.

Now, the concerns about security, crime, and social tension... I hear that all the time, especially from folks who are worried or scared about change. But honestly, most times those fears get blown way out of proportion. People use stories about crime to paint whole groups with one brush, and that’s not fair. There’s crime everywhere, no matter where people come from. If someone’s talking about actual data on crime rates, that’s worth looking at—but most of the time it’s just rumors and stereotypes.

As for terrorism, that’s even less likely, but gets used to scare people. We do need to be careful and keep communities safe, but we shouldn’t use fear as an excuse to treat people badly or shut the door on folks who need help.

The humanitarian side—giving refuge to people running from violence or poverty—that’s important. I think we have a responsibility to help where we can, because that’s just the right thing to do. But I also get that resources aren’t unlimited, and people want to know how helping others affects their own families.

People who are worried about jobs and income—that’s a real fear, especially for folks who are already struggling. If people feel like their jobs are being taken or their wages are dropping, it’s not wrong to ask questions. But we need real facts: Are immigrants actually causing that, or is it bigger issues like companies trying to cut costs or changes in the economy?

So, I find the arguments about jobs and culture reasonable, and I think the humanitarian side is important. The stuff about crime and terrorism needs real evidence—not just stories or fear. I believe more open dialogue and honest data would help. People need to talk, listen, and learn from each other, not just go off what they hear on TV.

Bottom line, there’s good and bad in every group. We need policies and conversations built on truth, not just fear or blame. That’s how I see it.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character18_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
If I’m speaking honestly as Character18_F, I wouldn’t go for either extreme—neither “let anybody in, no questions asked,” nor “close the doors tight.” Life is more complicated than that, and the people who end up suffering most from black-and-white policies are always the folks at the bottom. So, for me, it’s about finding a middle ground that’s fair to both the people already here and those who want a better life.

I’d lean toward a policy that mainly admits people based on job demand, but with some flexibility and safeguards. That means, if there’s a real need for workers in certain fields, especially jobs that locals aren’t filling, we should be open to letting immigrants fill those gaps. But that doesn’t mean companies can just bring in cheaper labor to undermine local workers or drive down wages. There need to be rules to protect everybody—locals and migrants—so folks aren’t being played against each other.

At the same time, I think setting some reasonable numerical limits makes sense. We can’t take in everyone at once; the system would get overwhelmed, and then nobody would get what they need. But those limits should be fair, transparent, and based on what’s really happening in the country—not just politics or panic.

I also believe in making room for humanitarian cases. If someone’s running from war, violence, or real hardship, this country should have a heart and find ways to help. That’s just what’s right, and that’s what I’d hope for if I was ever in that position.

The key is to have a system that’s flexible enough to respond to changes—both in the economy and in the world—but firm enough to protect workers’ rights and make sure everyone has a shot at building a life. And when people do come, we need to help them integrate—give language support, make sure they understand the laws and customs, and fight discrimination. That way, newcomers can really become part of the community instead of being pushed to the margins.

So, my ideal would be a mix: job-based entry, reasonable limits, room for humanitarian needs, and strong protections for both locals and newcomers. That’s how I think we get the fairest outcome for everybody.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character18_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character18_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Thank you for asking that.

Speaking as myself, J: Stepping into Character18_F’s shoes like this, I found myself really reflecting on how personal history and daily realities shape someone’s views. Her sense of fairness, her focus on who gets left out, and her refusal to see things in black and white—all of that came through strong. It reminded me that policy debates aren’t just about numbers and headlines; for people like Character18_F, they’re about dignity, survival, and community.

I think what I discovered most is how much empathy, caution, and hope are mixed together in her perspective. She wanted fairness for people like her—people who’ve struggled—but she also understood what it’s like to be judged or left out, so she didn’t want that for newcomers either. That balance isn’t easy, and I feel like I understand her toughness and compassion a bit more deeply now.

As for my own views, it made me realize that I probably lean a little more toward “everybody deserves a chance,” but I’m also more aware of why some people in my community feel cautious or worried. It’s not just about being “for” or “against” immigration—it’s about making policies that work for the folks who don’t have much to fall back on. That’s a deeper layer I maybe wouldn’t have sat with as much if I hadn’t been speaking as her.

Overall, this made me appreciate Character18_F’s honesty, practicality, and heart. I miss having her here, but I’m grateful we can keep her spirit alive by talking about these things the way she would’ve wanted.
